samasa.sense: in earth, the middle region and heaven alike
she who gives deeds their reward

morph.note: Past participle of आ + √दृ ‘to heed’, here active in sense, as often with this verb: ‘one who has given heed’, careful, devoted. अति intensifies it.
Possessive -इन् on सुकृत ‘a good deed’: सुकृतिन्, ‘one who has good deeds’; nom. sg. सुकृती.
A particle that asserts while inviting assent: ‘surely you are …, are you not?’

mantras.anvaya: (हे) देवि, सुकृती अत्यादृतः (सन्) प्रतिदिनं सकलानि धर्म्याणि कर्माणि सदा एव करोति, ततः च भवतीप्रसादात् स्वर्गं प्रयाति। तेन (हे) देवि, (त्वं) लोकत्रये अपि फलदा ननु।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two clauses with one subject (सुकृती): he does the deeds, and then reaches heaven through her grace. The conclusion (तेन … ननु) is a nominal sentence with ‘you’ understood.
mantras.lit: O Devī, the man of merit, with great care, every day always performs all righteous deeds; and then, through your grace, he goes to heaven. Therefore, O Devī, are you not the giver of fruit even in the three worlds?
mantras.tr: O Devī, the virtuous man performs every righteous deed, day after day, with devoted care, and then by your grace he goes to heaven. So is it not you, O Devī, who give the fruit of action in all three worlds?
mantras.tr_note: ननु is rendered as a question expecting ‘yes’.

comm.t: The good man’s deeds bear their fruit only through her grace (भवतीप्रसादात्). The gods conclude that she is the giver of reward in all three worlds, not in heaven alone.
Ritual duty is not set aside: it is done daily and with care. But its fruit comes from her favour, and this is why, in the Śākta tradition, devotion is joined to duty rather than replacing it.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) names the Goddess स्वर्गापवर्गदा (name 764), ‘giver of heaven and of release’. The Devī Māhātmya speaks here of heaven and of fruit in the three worlds; release is the subject of 4.9 (मुक्तिहेतुः).

samasa.alt: It can also be taken as a collective, ‘of all creatures’ (अशेषाणां जन्तूनाम्); the singular is then distributive. The sense is the same.

samasa.sense: by the healthy and untroubled, those not in distress

samasa.vigraha: दारिद्र्यं च दुःखं च भयं च दारिद्र्यदुःखभयानि; तानि हरति इति दारिद्र्यदुःखभयहारिणी, तत्सम्बुद्धौ

samasa.literal: O you who take away poverty, sorrow and fear
samasa.sense: O remover of want, grief and fear
samasa.alt: दारिद्र्यदुःख may be read as a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa, ‘the sorrow of poverty’ (दारिद्र्यस्य दुःखम्), giving two things removed instead of three; the list of three is the usual reading.

samasa.literal: for the doing of help to all

morph.note: A passive participle with the force of a condition: ‘(when you are) remembered’. In line 2 its agent is स्वस्थैः; in line 1 the agent is left open, so anyone at all who remembers her.
Reduplicated present of √दा (juhotyādi class): द-दा-सि ‘you give’.
Vocative of the feminine of हारिन् (√हृ + -इन्, ‘taking away’), which adds -ई: हारिणी, voc. हारिणि.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) दुर्गे, स्मृता (त्वम्) अशेषजन्तोः भीतिं हरसि; स्वस्थैः स्मृता (त्वम्) अतीव शुभां मतिं ददासि। (हे) दारिद्र्यदुःखभयहारिणि, सर्वोपकारकरणाय सदा आर्द्रचित्ता त्वदन्या का (अस्ति)?
mantras.anvaya_en: Two parallel clauses, each conditioned by स्मृता; then a rhetorical question, ‘who other than you …?’, whose answer is ‘no one’.
mantras.lit: O Durgā, remembered, you take away the fear of every creature; remembered by those at ease, you give an exceedingly auspicious understanding. O remover of poverty, sorrow and fear, who other than you is always tender-hearted for doing good to all?
mantras.tr: O Durgā, when you are remembered you take away the fear of every creature; remembered by those at ease, you give a mind turned wholly to the good. Remover of poverty, sorrow and fear — who but you has a heart ever tender, ready to help all?

comm.t: Two kinds of people remember her: any creature in fear, whose fear she removes, and those at ease (स्वस्थैः), to whom she gives a good understanding. The verse ends by asking who else is so tender towards all; the unspoken answer is no one.

Remembrance alone (स्मृता) is enough; no rite or offering is named. The verse is one of the seven gathered in the Saptaślokī Durgā, a short devotional selection from the Saptaśatī, and it is among the best known of the whole text.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the names दुर्गा (190), दुःखहन्त्री (191) and भयापहा (121), close to this verse’s दुर्गे and दारिद्र्यदुःखभयहारिणि. The parallel is one of epithets; the two hymns are separate works.

samasa.sense: a warrior’s death on the field

morph.note: Imperative with the particle नाम has concessive force: ‘let them indeed do (sin)’, i.e. ‘granted that they sin’. It sets up the contrast with प्रयान्तु ‘(yet) let them go (to heaven)’.
Accusative singular of दिव् (nominative द्यौः), ‘sky, heaven’, feminine in this sense.
Present of √हन् with two prefixes: हन् + सि → हंसि (the n becomes anusvāra before s). The 2nd person addresses the Goddess directly.

mantras.anvaya: एभिः हतैः जगत् सुखम् उपैति; तथा एते चिराय नरकाय पापं कुर्वन्तु नाम, (तथापि) संग्राममृत्युम् अधिगम्य दिवं प्रयान्तु — इति मत्वा नूनं (हे) देवि, (त्वम्) अहितान् विनिहंसि।
mantras.anvaya_en: Lines 1–3 are the Goddess’s thought as the gods imagine it, closed by इति; the main clause is मत्वा … विनिहंसि.
mantras.lit: ‘By these being slain the world attains happiness; and likewise these — granted they do sin (leading) to hell for long — having met death in battle, let them go to heaven’: having thought thus, surely, you strike down the enemies, O Devī.
mantras.tr: ‘With these slain, the world will find happiness; and though they have earned a long hell by their sins, let them meet death in battle and go to heaven’ — surely it is with this thought, O Devī, that you strike your enemies down.
mantras.tr_note: कुर्वन्तु नाम (‘let them do, granted’) is rendered as a concession, ‘though they have earned … by their sins’.

comm.t: The gods explain why she kills: the world is freed, and the slain asuras themselves, whatever their sins, reach heaven through death in battle at her hands. One act serves both the world and the killed.

That death in battle opens heaven belongs to the warrior ethic of the epics and Purāṇas; the hymn applies it to the Goddess’s enemies. With 4.19–20 it builds the theme the gods state outright in 4.21: her compassion reaches even her enemies (वैरिष्वपि … दया).
A modern reading: the verse refuses to divide beings into those who deserve good and those who do not. Even her destruction is imagined as a form of care.
